Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement. 
On November 20, 2026, Energy Transfer LP (the “Partnership”) completed its previously reported underwritten public offering (the “Offering”) of $900,000,000 aggregate principal amount of its 5.450% Senior Notes due 2032 (the “2032 Notes”), $900,000,000 aggregate principal amount of its 5.900% Senior Notes due 2037 (the “2037 Notes”) and $900,000,000 aggregate principal amount of its 6.550% Senior Notes due 2057 (the “2057 Notes” and, together with the 2032 Notes and the 2037 Notes, the “Notes”). The Notes were issued under the Indenture, dated as of December 14, 2022 (the “Indenture”), between the Partnership and U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, as trustee, as supplemented by the Thirteenth Supplemental Indenture, dated as of November 20, 2026 (the “Thirteenth Supplemental Indenture”). 
The Offering was registered under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”), pursuant to a Registration Statement on Form S-3ASR (File No. 333-279982) of the Partnership, which became effective on June 6, 2024, as amended by Post-Effective Amendment No. 1 thereto and as supplemented by the Prospectus Supplement, dated November 5, 2026 (together with the accompanying prospectus, dated June 5, 2024, the “Prospectus Supplement”), filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission pursuant to Rule 424(b) of the Securities Act on November 6, 2026 and given a filing date of November 9, 2026. The legal opinion related to the Notes is included as Exhibit 5.1 to this Current Report on Form 8-K. 
The terms of the Notes and the Thirteenth Supplemental Indenture are further described in the Prospectus Supplement under the captions “Description of the Notes” and “Description of Debt Securities.” Such descriptions do not purport to be complete and are qualified by reference to the Indenture and the Thirteenth Supplemental Indenture, copies of which are filed as Exhibit 4.1 and Exhibit 4.2, respectively, to this Current Report on Form 8-K and incorporated by reference into this Item 1.01.

Item 5.02 Departure of Directors or Certain Officers; Election of Directors; Appointment of Certain Officers; Compensatory Arrangements of Certain Officers.
On November 18, 2026, the Board of Directors of LyondellBasell Industries N.V. (the “Company”), following recommendation of the Compensation & Talent Development Committee, approved one-time retention awards for certain members of the Company’s Executive Committee. The awards are intended to promote leadership continuity and retention during the Company’s ongoing portfolio transformation.
Kimberly Foley, the Company’s Executive Vice President, Olefins and Polyolefins and Trading, will receive a $2,000,000 cash retention award. The award is separate from, and in addition to, Ms. Foley’s regular annual incentive compensation and is payable following her continued employment with the Company through December 31, 2027.
Agustin Izquierdo, the Company’s Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, has received a one-time restricted stock unit (“RSU”) award with a target value of $750,000. The RSUs will cliff vest on the third anniversary of the grant date, generally subject to Mr. Izquierdo’s continued employment with the Company through the vesting date and is in addition to his regular annual long-term incentive award.
The foregoing descriptions of the retention awards do not purport to be complete and are qualified in their entirety by reference to the applicable award agreements, copies of which are included as Exhibits 10.1 and 10.2 to this Current Report on Form 8-K and incorporated herein by reference.

1. Relationship to Plan and Company Agreements.

Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners 
For release at 4:15 p.m. EST 
 Share 
The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. 
The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail. 
"I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy." 
This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University. 
Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations.

The U.S. Economy in Global Context 
 Governor Lisa D. Cook 
At the XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile 
 Share 
 Watch Live 
Thank you, Governor Costa, for that kind introduction and for the invitation to deliver this keynote address and to participate in the 29th Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile today.1 It is a distinct privilege to be back in Santiago. I first came to Chile between my second and third years as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley after completing a summer as an intern at the World Bank. I was on a quest to determine whether economic growth in Latin America or in another region of the world would be the subject of my dissertation. It piqued my interest in inflation targeting, a sound fiscal framework, and now, of course, how to think about the economic forces reshaping the global economy. I am grateful for the chance to continue to learn from your experience and to share some of my own thinking. 
I want to begin by acknowledging a fact that may seem obvious but is easy to overlook in the day-to-day work of setting monetary policy: The U.S. economy does not sit in isolation. As a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, my mandate is domestic—to promote maximum employment and price stability in the United States. But achieving that mandate requires that I pay careful attention to global developments, including economic and financial developments in Chile and across Latin America. The forces reconfiguring your economies are, in many cases, identical to the forces reconfiguring ours, even if they arrive on our respective shores somewhat differently. 
Geopolitics and Trade
Let me start with geopolitical events. Over the past several years, the global economy has absorbed a remarkable sequence of shocks. Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted energy and commodity markets worldwide. The conflict in the Middle East pushed up energy prices again this year, and experts have warned that damaged infrastructure and depleted inventories could keep oil prices elevated for an extended period. These are not simply North American concerns. Oil is a globally traded commodity, and a conflict that drives up the price of oil in Houston drives it up in Santiago, as well. The precise transmission differs across countries, depending on whether they are net energy importers or exporters, but few economies have been insulated. 
A related story applies to trade. Over the past two years, the U.S. has raised tariffs on a wide range of imports, and considerable uncertainty remains about where tariff levels will ultimately settle. In the U.S., the effects of tariffs on inflation appear to have moderated, even as uncertainty about future trade policy persists. China, too, has increased trade restrictions, limiting exports of critical minerals for which it supplies a large fraction of the world's production. These minerals are a crucial input, and uncertainty is rising around the world about access to them. I raise this not to make a judgment about trade policy—that is not my role—but because such shifts inevitably reverberate across the global economy. When trade relationships between major economies are altered, other countries must decide how to respond: whether to deepen commercial ties elsewhere, reconfigure supply chains, or wait for greater clarity before committing to new investment. These are decisions playing out in boardrooms and finance ministries around the world right now, including, I suspect, in some of the economies represented in this room. 
The Global AI Buildout
The third global force I want to highlight—and the one I will spend the most time on—is the extraordinary buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure now underway around the world. 
While at the Board, I have spent much of my career as an economist studying innovation, including AI. Now, I spend considerable time talking with contacts in the U.S. and around the world about how AI is evolving and being used. I have spoken on several occasions about how I view AI—as a general-purpose technology, on par with or perhaps exceeding the steam engine, electrification, and the internet in its potential to transform how we work, innovate, and grow. This technology could bring a productivity boom unparalleled in generations.2 At the same time, I worry deeply about our shared risks resulting from the technology, such as the specter of a painful labor market transition or cyber and financial-stability risks. Uncertainty abounds. 
In the U.S., AI has catalyzed a historic wave of investment. Companies have announced plans for more than $2 trillion in specific data center construction projects. So far, only a fraction of this has been realized.3 This investment is already showing up in output data. And there is evidence of spillovers to other parts of the economy—in the price of chips and high-tech equipment, construction wages, and electricity costs. 
What I want to stress today is that this is not simply a North American phenomenon. By some estimates, roughly one-half of the world's data-center capacity now under construction is being built outside the U.S.4 The AI buildout is a global undertaking, and it is reshaping economies—including economies in this region—in ways that are only beginning to be understood. 
Chile and its neighbors sit at an interesting intersection of this story. This country is the world's largest producer of copper and the second-largest producer of lithium—two minerals increasingly central to the infrastructure that AI requires, including power transmission and energy-storage systems.5 This raises some questions to which I do not think any of us has a full answer. As demand for these minerals rises and falls with the pace of the global AI buildout, does this represent a new source of growth for resource-rich economies or a new source of volatility layered on top of already volatile commodity cycles? As capital flows toward AI infrastructure and related resource extraction around the world, what are the implications for smaller open economies managing capital flows, exchange rates, and financial stability? 
Corresponding to the buildout in physical infrastructure, adoption of AI tools by businesses and individuals is spreading quickly as well, albeit unevenly across countries. Recent work tracking the share of the working-age population using generative AI tools finds diffusion ranging from roughly 25 to 45 percent across higher-income economies, including Chile. These figures already exceed the pace of adoption we saw for personal computers at a comparable stage.6 This matters a great deal for growth, because wider adoption of a general-purpose technology is ultimately how its productivity gains would be realized throughout an economy—gains that, in principle, could be sizeable. 
Simultaneously, researchers have raised questions about the distribution of gains across countries. Recent analysis from the International Monetary Fund suggests that advanced economies may be positioned to capture a disproportionate share of global AI-driven productivity growth over the next decade, relative to developing economies.7 If this pattern holds, it raises important questions: Where in the distribution will countries like Chile wind up, and what might determine distributional outcomes? 
Finally, on the AI buildout, I would like to address AI and the labor market, the focus of today's conference. As with any major new technology, AI is likely to cause a shift in the labor market with jobs and job tasks being replaced by AI, and new jobs—many of which we cannot yet conceive of—being created. Ultimately, history has shown that human innovation will likely lead to a successful transition, with permanent job loss unlikely. However, I am very aware of the nonzero probability that this transition could take time and that job losses due to AI could precede new job creation. 
In the U.S., labor markets appear resilient to date, but AI adoption is still in its early stages, and I think it is too soon to feel comforted. We do see that some workers have already been affected by AI. For instance, there is already some evidence that labor demand has cooled for coding jobs in the software industry and in simultaneous translation. In addition, younger adults are experiencing prolonged job searches, which some attribute to nascent pressure from AI on entry-level positions. As AI adoption spreads, younger workers may continue to be disproportionately affected, and firms may need to take innovative and creative steps to train their future workforce. 
I am watching carefully the speed and acceleration of AI adoption across sectors and noting evidence of the changing mix of jobs within firms. New types of tasks and jobs are already being created, and I remain hopeful that job creation will be able to keep pace with job destruction. 
I will now turn to my outlook on the U.S. economy. 
U.S. Economic Outlook
Overall economic growth in the U.S. is strong—and accelerating. The labor market remains solid, and, of great concern to me, inflation is well above the Fed's 2 percent target and has been for 67 months. I will start my forecast, as I typically do, with the price-stability side of our dual mandate, because, given the current state of the economy, this is my focus. Then, I will give my views on the path of monetary policy. One theme I want to emphasize is that waiting to act when a policy adjustment is required has a cost. 
Inflation
Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, has exceeded the 2 percent target described in our framework for nearly six years. Based on U.S. inflation data released last week, it is estimated that the 12-month change in the PCE price index was 3.8 percent in October. The 12-month change in core prices—which exclude volatile food and energy costs—was 3.2 percent in October. The core measure underscores that, while energy is a significant contributor to inflation, the sources of price pressure facing American families are increasingly varied. 
Inflation soared in 2021 and 2022 because of supply disruptions and surging demand following the reopening of the U.S. and economies around the world as the global pandemic abated. The Fed, much like other central banks, responded by aggressively raising interest rates to fight inflation. I supported those actions as soon as I joined the Fed. From the middle of 2022 until the early part of last year, inflation moved down and appeared to be on a sustainable path back toward the 2 percent objective. However, a series of economic shocks over the past 18 months—including significant changes to trade policy, geopolitical developments, and massive investment in technological infrastructure—partially reversed that progress. On November 20, 2026, American Airlines Group Inc. (the “Company”) announced that David G. Seymour will cease serving as the Company’s Chief Operating Officer of the Company and American Airlines, Inc. (“American”) on December 31, 2026 (the “Transition Date”).
Pursuant to the terms of the transition and separation letter agreement entered into with Mr. Seymour as of November 20, 2026 (the “Transition Agreement”), following the Transition Date, Mr. Seymour is expected to continue to provide services to the Company as a strategic advisor for up to three months during which he will be paid a base salary at the rate of $25,000 per month and remain eligible for all Company benefits provided to its Executive Vice Presidents, including Company-sponsored healthcare insurance.
Subject to the terms of the Transition Agreement, Mr. Seymour will continue to remain eligible for his 2026 annual bonus and subject to his delivery of an effective release of claims and continued compliance with his obligations under his previously disclosed Restrictive Covenants Agreement with the Company dated as of September 20, 2023, the Company will provide Mr. Seymour with the severance payments and benefits pursuant to the covered termination provisions set forth in his previously disclosed Severance Agreement with the Company dated as of September 20, 2023, in accordance with the terms set forth therein.
The foregoing description of Mr. Seymour’s Transition Agreement is qualified in its entirety by the text of the agreement, a copy of which will be filed as an exhibit to the Company’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2026, and incorporated herein by reference.
In connection with Mr. Seymour’s retirement, the Company also announced that JonCarlo Gulbranson will be appointed Executive Vice President, Chief Operations Officer, effective January 1, 2027. Mr. Gulbranson currently serves as American’s Senior Vice President, Operations, leading the airline’s airport, flight and inflight operations, as well as operations planning and analytics, product management and the Integrated Operations Center, which oversees the airline’s day-to-day operation.
Mr. Gulbranson, 49, has served in his current role since August 2026. Prior to that, Mr. Gulbranson served as American’s Senior Vice President of Airport Operations beginning in February 2021, where he led the global airports team through the challenges of COVID-19 and the post-pandemic travel recovery. He also served as Vice President of Operations Planning and Control Center beginning in August 2019, as well as Vice President of Customer Care beginning in July 2018, leading American’s Global Reservations, Customer Relations and Service Recovery contact centers. Mr. Gulbranson began his airline career in 2000 at Northwest Airlines and joined US Airways in 2008.
In connection with his new role, effective as of January 1, 2027, Mr. Gulbranson’s compensation will include a base salary of $800,000, an annual incentive program target opportunity of 125% of his base salary, and a long-term incentive (“LTI”) target award valued at $2,400,000 to be granted in 2027, consistent with the terms of the Company’s long-term incentive program. LTIs include performance share awards (accounting for 50% of target LTI value) and restricted stock units (accounting for 50% of target LTI value). Payouts on both the annual incentive program and the performance share awards will be based on the achievement of pre-established performance targets. Mr. Gulbranson remains eligible for benefits similar to those of other Company executive officers, including flight benefits, and participation in the Company’s health, welfare and retirement plans. Mr. Gulbranson will be eligible to enter into the Company’s severance agreement for executive-level employees providing for eighteen months of each of the following compensation components on an involuntary termination: base salary, short-term incentive target payout, continued vesting of outstanding equity awards within the severance period, COBRA payment and travel benefits. Receipt and continuation of these benefits will be contingent on Mr. Gulbranson’s execution of, and continued compliance with, the terms of the Company’s restrictive covenants agreement, which among other things, will subject Mr. Gulbranson to an eighteen-month post-employment non-competition covenant and a twenty-four month post-employment non-solicitation covenant.
There are no arrangements or understandings between Mr. Gulbranson and any other person pursuant to which he will be appointed to serve in his new role. There are no family relationships between Mr. Gulbranson and any director or executive officer of the Company or American nor does Mr. Gulbranson have a direct or indirect material interest in any “related party” transaction required to be disclosed pursuant to Item 404(a) of Regulation S-K.

Opening Remarks 
 Governor Christopher J. Waller 
At the 2026 College Fed Challenge Finals, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, D.C. 
 Share 
Thank you, Robin, and welcome, students and teachers, to the Federal Reserve Board.1 
We are gathered for the finals of the annual College Fed Challenge, a tradition begun 23 years ago under Chairman Alan Greenspan. The challenge is to prepare and present a monetary policy recommendation that will best promote the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment. Students on the seven teams that will compete today represent the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Chicago; Cleveland State University; Harvard College; the University of Maryland, College Park; Pennsylvania State University; and St. Lawrence University. 
Let me start by congratulating all of the students here today, and your faculty advisers, for advancing to the finals by winning preliminary rounds of the competition. A record 141 schools participated this year, from 34 states. It is incredibly gratifying to think of the number of young people motivated to learn about the Federal Reserve's role in promoting a healthy economy. 
A few weeks from now, my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and I will be sitting at this same table, facing the same challenge you face today. Like you, we will be examining publicly available data on economic and financial conditions and will apply our understanding of how monetary policy influences those conditions to render our best judgment of the policy stance that best furthers the Fed's goals. 
Crucial to that decision will be clearly explaining the Committee's actions and intentions to the public—the same task that you will face later this morning, when you present your recommendations to our judges. As I hope you have learned, clear communication is essential because monetary policy works to a considerable extent by influencing the public's view of current and future economic and financial conditions. 
Monetary policy has evolved since this competition began in 2003. At that time, the FOMC relied on a single tool to influence financial conditions and the broader economy—it set a target for the federal funds rate. In the years since, the Committee expanded its toolkit with unconventional policy tools. 
In an important way, the competition you will engage in today is very much like what the FOMC does at its meetings. On December 8, my 18 FOMC colleagues and I will each present our view of the economic outlook, and on December 9, our view of the proper stance of monetary policy. Before we express those views to the public, we communicate with each other, presenting evidence, testing hypotheses, and making arguments that will ultimately help us arrive at a consensus that is summarized in our postmeeting statement. Every monetary policy speech I give has its origins in this room, in the argument I make here, and the extent to which that argument holds up to what I hear from my colleagues. When I engage in the essential task of explaining monetary policy to the public, I am really doing the same thing that I do here at FOMC meetings. And very much what you will do today. Present the evidence. Make an argument. Persuade. 
I hope your preparations for this event have added to your understanding of the economy and the Federal Reserve's role and perhaps will even spur some of you to pursue further study of economics and finance. Among the talented individuals who are participating in today's challenge, I hope there are some who may one day contribute to our understanding of the economy and the work of the Fed. But I hope that all of you have benefited from this experience by adding to your knowledge and developing research, analytical, and communication skills that will help you in whatever careers you choose. 
I'd like to thank the judges who have given their time and offered their expertise and experience to the evaluation of each team's work. They represent the very best of the Federal Reserve. From the Board we have Sriya Anbil, who is an economist in the Board's Division of Monetary Affairs; Karen Pence, who is a deputy director in the Division of Research and Statistics; and Brian Doyle, who is a deputy director in the Division of International Finance. And from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas we have Sam Schulhofer-Wohl, a senior vice president and senior adviser to president Lorie Logan. 
Also, let me again thank the faculty advisers of each of the seven teams for helping guide, motivate, and prepare today's finalists. And thanks also to the Federal Reserve's economic education staff who have organized the Fed Challenge this year and to all the judges who volunteered their time to make it possible. 
I am looking forward to a spirited competition, and I wish you all the best of luck. 
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text

PayPal Announces Executive Leadership Appointments to Advance Three-Year Strategy 
New leaders bring deep experience across financial services, technology and enterprise operations to accelerate execution 
San Jose, Calif., November 20, 2026—PayPal Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: PYPL) today announced several
executive leadership appointments. This follows several months of strategic planning to establish clear strategies across PayPal’s core businesses, simplify its operating model and align leadership accountability with the company’s
long-term priorities. 
“We’ve made significant progress in defining where we want to take PayPal and how we will compete and win,” said
Enrique Lores, President and CEO of PayPal. “With our three-year strategies in place, our focus is now on execution. These appointments bring together experienced leaders with the capabilities to accelerate innovation, strengthen our
businesses and deliver greater value to our customers and shareholders.” 
Key leadership appointments include: 
 | 
 | •
 | 
 | 
Claire Bramley, EVP & Chief Financial Officer. Bramley will succeed Jamie
Miller, Chief Financial and Operating Officer. She will join on February 1, working closely with Miller throughout February to ensure a smooth transition and business continuity. Miller has guided the company through a period of
extraordinary change, including leading through a CEO transition and playing an instrumental role in defining the new strategy. 
Bramley joins from Xero, the global small-business platform, where she has served as Chief Financial Officer since April 2025. At Xero, she
helped lead the company’s U.S. expansion, including its acquisition of U.S. payments platform, Melio. She brings extensive financial and strategic leadership experience in the technology industry. Before joining Xero, she was CFO at Teradata
and held senior finance roles at HP. 
 | 
 | •
 | 
 | 
Kartik Mani, President and Head of Consumer Financial Services and Venmo. Mani will join PayPal from
American Express, where he currently serves as President of Global Network and Partner Services. He previously led Citi’s Consumer Banking business across Asia and EMEA and American Express’ global lending business. He brings extensive
experience building and scaling card, credit and network businesses. Mani will oversee PayPal’s consumer financial services strategy, including Venmo, with a focus on deepening customer engagement and expanding financial services offerings
across the enterprise. Alexis Sowa who has demonstrated outstanding leadership in Venmo will continue in her role as General Manager of Venmo, reporting to Mani. 
 | 
 | •
 | 
 | 
Suzan Kereere, President and Head of Payment Services & Crypto. Kereere, who
currently leads Global Markets, will assume responsibility for PayPal’s Payment Services & Crypto business, succeeding Jeff Pomeroy, who has served as interim lead and will continue to manage Payment Services & Platforms,
reporting to Kereere. As head of Global Markets, Kereere has focused on more profitable merchant relationships, deeper customer relationships and faster market-level decision-making. With much of this foundational work now in place, Kereere will
draw on her extensive commercial and operating experience, including her deep payments industry expertise during her time at Fiserv, to lead PS&C. 
 | 
 | •
 | 
 | 
Juan Rio, EVP of AI Business Transformation and Operations. Rio will join PayPal on November 30,
2026, from Brightstar.AI, where he serves as Managing Director and Chief Delivery Officer. He leads AI transformation initiatives across Brightstar Capital Partners’ portfolio companies, focused on improving profitability and operational
performance. Rio brings extensive experience in large-scale operational transformation, including the integration of T-Mobile and Sprint. Rio will lead PayPal’s AI, cost simplification and enterprise
operating effectiveness initiatives. 
Frank Keller will continue to lead Checkout Solutions & PayPal, including branded
checkout, where our merchant and consumer strategy is driving improved performance through better experiences, presentment and consumer marketing. 
PayPal
also announced that Aaron Webster, Chief Risk Officer, will depart the company. Ratinder Bedi, SVP of Credit and Fraud Risk, will serve as interim head of the Risk organization, while the company conducts a search for a permanent
successor. 
In addition, we announced the appointment of a new Board of Director, Brian J. Lee earlier today. Lee brings more than three decades of
financial services experience, including serving as Chief Risk Officer at Goldman Sachs for six years. 
PayPal will provide an update on progress against
its three-year strategic plans on its fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call. 
About PayPal 
PayPal has been revolutionizing commerce globally for more than 25 years. Creating innovative experiences that make moving money, selling and shopping simple,
personalized and secure, PayPal empowers consumers and businesses in approximately 200 markets to join and thrive in the global economy. For more information, visit https://www.paypal.com, https://about.pypl.com, and https://investor.pypl.com.

SPEECH
Acting in time
Keynote speech by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the 36th Frankfurt European Banking Congress
Frankfurt am Main, 20 November 2026
It is a pleasure to be back at this congress. This is the eighth time I have spoken here as President of the ECB, and it will sadly be the last.
In preparing for today, I reread those speeches. The topics have varied, from growth and inflation to capital markets and the Single Market.
But one concern runs through all of them: how to make Europe stronger, so that its prosperity is driven by its own strengths and less exposed to decisions taken elsewhere.
For many years, the challenges we discussed here were old ones. We had fallen short of our ambitions for the Single Market. Our growth relied too heavily on external demand for an economy of our size, and our competitiveness was slowly eroding.
Those challenges have not gone away. But in recent years, new ones have been layered on top. Dependencies that we once saw as a normal part of an open economy, from critical raw materials to technology, can now be used against us. That has made economic sovereignty a challenge in its own right.
The old challenges and the new ones have something in common.
Five centuries ago, Machiavelli compared the problems of states to a fever that, at the start, is “easy to cure but difficult to detect” and, in time, becomes “easy to detect but difficult to cure”.
Both kinds of challenge are of this sort. By the time everyone can see the need to act, the best time to act has usually passed.
Acting early, before the case is obvious, is one of the hardest things a policymaker has to do. It means paying a price up front for a distant pay-off. And if nothing goes wrong, those who acted can easily appear to have paid that price for nothing.
Today I would like to reflect on how Europe can still act early, drawing on how we have approached this at the ECB and on what I have learned along the way.
Why Europe acts in some crises but not others
It is often said that Europe only moves in a crisis. Jean Monnet wrote that Europe would be forged in crises, and would be the sum of the solutions adopted for them. The idea was that Europe has a kind of in-built inertia that only a crisis can overcome.
My experience of the past seven years is that this is only partly true. Europe responds decisively to some crises and hesitantly to others.
When events convince us that the world has changed, we act. During my term, I have watched Europe break one taboo after another.
Before the pandemic, few believed that the EU would ever borrow on a large scale in its own name. But once we accepted that no country could recover on its own, we created a recovery fund financed by common debt to the tune of €800 billion.
Europe was also said to be unable to take its own security seriously. Yet when Germany concluded that it would have to take on more of its own defence, it made the biggest change to its defence spending in generations. At the European level, we also agreed on Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which offers up to €150 billion in loans for joint defence procurement. And after decades of neutrality, Finland and Sweden joined NATO.
Nor did many expect Europe to act as a geopolitical power. Yet it is now Ukraine’s largest supporter. And when it became clear that Europe would have to bear more of the cost, the countries ready to act found a new way to borrow together on Ukraine’s behalf, even though not every country was ready to take part. Hence the coalition of the willing.
What made these steps possible? In each case, the cost of inaction was there for all to see, and it was plainly greater than the cost of acting. Once we were convinced of that, our institutions did not hold us back.
Our difficulties arise when a crisis moves slowly. The cost of inaction is then just as real, but it is far less visible. It builds up a little each year, and no single moment forces a decision. Meanwhile, the cost of acting is certain and has to be paid straight away.
Both the old challenges and the new ones are of this kind.
Take capital markets. We have all agreed for more than a decade that Europe needs a capital markets union. But building it means taking on vested interests now, for gains that arrive years later.
Each year without it, more of our savings are invested abroad and more of our growing firms look elsewhere for funding. Yet no single year’s loss is large enough to overcome the resistance to change.
We have seen this again in recent weeks. The Council has just agreed its position on strengthening the supervision of capital markets, which is welcome. But the position weakens the European supervisor’s ability to take effective decisions and includes too many carve-outs.
Our dependencies raise the same problem. Reducing them means paying for new capacity now, against a threat that may never materialise. One recent estimate suggests that raising Europe’s share of the world’s AI computing capacity from around 5% to 15% by 2030 would require investment of around €1.3 trillion.[1]
But as long as we can buy computing power from foreign providers and frontier AI models remain available to us, the case for paying that price is hard to make.
In both, the cost of inaction is real, whether it is a loss we are already suffering or a danger we may face tomorrow. But it rarely becomes visible enough to build the broad consensus for change that we found for the pandemic or for Ukraine.
This is the central problem of European policymaking. We can see the problem early, but we can act only once it has become impossible to ignore. And by then, almost by definition, it is too late. Lost industries are very hard to win back, and once a dependency has been used against us, our sovereignty is already exposed.
Think of the euro area debt crisis. The scale of Greece’s difficulties was clear long before Europe acted decisively to strengthen its institutions. We paid a much higher price than if we had acted earlier, including a six-quarter recession.
We often hear that policymakers in Europe do not understand the problems they face. I think they do. The difficulty is that they are asked to impose visible costs on their citizens today, for benefits that will only become apparent over time, before a majority is convinced that action is needed.
These are among the hardest decisions in public life, and I have a great deal of sympathy for those who have to take them.
At the ECB, we have had to take some of them too.
Acting early at the ECB
Economic sovereignty is not an objective in itself for us. Our primary objective is price stability, and the Treaty also gives us the tasks of issuing money and promoting the smooth operation of payment systems. But a changing world bears directly on those tasks, and during my term it has confronted us with slow-moving risks of our own.
We have faced decisions of this kind in three areas. In each, we had to choose whether to invest early in something whose value would only become clear later.
The first area was retail payments.
Since the euro was introduced, Europeans have had a single means of payment that works everywhere in the euro area: euro cash. But for card payments, we have relied on providers from outside Europe. International card schemes handle more than 60% of our card payments, and 14 of the 21 euro area countries have no domestic scheme at all.[2]
For a long time, this did not seem to matter, because cash was still the dominant means of payment. The international schemes worked well, and no one had ever cut Europe off.
The private sector tried more than once to build a European alternative, but each attempt ran into the same vicious circle: merchants will not adopt a scheme that few customers use, and customers will not use one that few merchants accept.
But cash is playing a smaller role as more of our spending moves online, where more than a third of our day-to-day spending now takes place.[3] And the geopolitical climate has changed. We have already seen judges of the International Criminal Court living in Europe, some of them European citizens, lose the use of their bank cards overnight.
So we concluded that Europe needed a digital equivalent of cash: the digital euro.
It will give Europeans a means of payment that runs on European infrastructure. And as legal tender, it will have to be accepted throughout the euro area wherever digital payments are possible, which will break the vicious circle in a way that private initiatives could not. Private payment providers will then have open rails on which to compete.
Because a project of this scale takes years to build, we had to start well before the need became pressing. If the legislation is adopted by the end of this year, we aim to be ready for a first issuance in 2029.
The second area was wholesale markets.
With blockchain technology, securities can now be tokenised, so that they are issued, traded and settled on a single platform. With the right framework, tokenisation offers a chance to build a genuine single market in digital assets, integrated from the start. For Europe, that is a huge opportunity.
But the window for seizing it is limited. The market for tokenised assets is still small, worth around €23 billion worldwide in March, but it was five times its size a year earlier.[4] As it grows, its standards and practices will take shape.
If they develop separately, the market could split into platforms that follow different rules and cannot settle with one another. And as our capital markets have taught us, once standards and practices have diverged, they are very hard to bring back together.
That is why, in September, we launched Pontes, which allows tokenised transactions to settle in central bank money on Eurosystem infrastructure, under European rules. Every platform now has access to a common settlement asset, so liquidity no longer has to be divided between them. Earlier this month, the European Stability Mechanism settled a €1 billion digitally native bond on Pontes.
Through Appia, we are working with market participants towards an integrated European market, including common standards. But infrastructure alone is not enough. Common rules will be needed too, and those lie with legislators.
The third area was the international role of the euro.
For most of its history, the ECB took a neutral view of the euro’s international role. Shortly before my term began, it moved to a more supportive line, and during my term we have acted on it. A stronger international role for the euro matters for our monetary policy, and it can support Europe’s growth and sovereignty in the world we now face.
Europe faces large investment needs, from defence to the technologies on which our autonomy depends, and a currency that investors around the world want to hold lowers the cost of financing them. In a world of more frequent shocks, the more of our trade is invoiced in euro, the less exposed we are to swings in exchange rates.
So, where it supports our own mandate, we have made the euro easier to use abroad.
We are linking TIPS, our instant payment system, with fast payment systems in other regions. We have also strengthened our international liquidity lines as a backstop. In February we made EUREP, our repo facility for central banks, permanent and open to central banks worldwide. More than 30 central banks have already expressed interest. And we are working to keep our swap lines fit for purpose in a more fragmented world. They will be more accessible, too.

CONSUMER PRICE INDEX - OCTOBER 2026
The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October 
after rising 0.6 percent in September, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. 
The index for shelter rose 0.3 percent in October, accounting for over thirty percent of the monthly all items increase. 
The food index increased 0.5 percent in October, as the food at home index rose 0.4 percent and the food away from home 
index increased 0.5 percent. The index for energy increased 0.7 percent over the month following a 5.2-percent increase 
in September. 
The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in October, as it did in September and August. Indexes that 
increased over the month include recreation, medical care, motor vehicle insurance, household furnishings and operations, 
and education. Conversely, the index for used cars and trucks and the index for communication were among the small number 
of major indexes that decreased in October.

Food
The index for food rose 0.5 percent in October after being unchanged in September. The food at home index increased 0.4 
percent over the month. Four of the six major grocery store food group indexes increased in October, while one index 
decreased. The index for other food at home increased 0.7 percent in October, as the index for snacks rose 1.0 percent. 
The meats, poultry, fish, and eggs index increased 0.5 percent over the month, as the beef index rose 0.9 percent. The 
index for fruits and vegetables and the index for dairy and related products each increased 0.6 percent in October. 
In contrast, the nonalcoholic beverages index decreased 0.3 percent in October, after rising 0.9 percent in September. 
The index for cereals and bakery products was unchanged over the month.
The food away from home index rose 0.5 percent in October. The index for full service meals rose 0.7 percent, and the 
index for limited service meals increased 0.4 percent over the month.
Energy
The index for energy increased 0.7 percent in October after rising 5.2 percent in September. The gasoline index increased 
1.0 percent over the month, after advancing 9.1 percent the previous month. (Before seasonal adjustment, gasoline prices 
decreased 0.7 percent in October.) The index for electricity rose 0.9 percent over the month. In contrast, the natural 
gas index decreased 0.8 percent in October.
All items less food and energy
The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in October, as it did in September and August. The shelter 
index increased 0.3 percent over the month after rising 0.4 percent in September. The index for owners' equivalent rent 
rose 0.3 percent in October, and the index for rent increased 0.2 percent. The lodging away from home index rose 0.6 
percent in October after rising 2.0 percent the previous month.
The index for recreation increased 0.8 percent over the month after rising 0.5 percent in September. The motor vehicle 
insurance index rose 0.7 percent in October, and the household furnishings and operations index increased 0.2 percent. 
The index for education increased 0.3 percent in October, and the index for new vehicles rose 0.2 percent. The personal 
care index, the airline fares index, and the apparel index also increased over the month.
The medical care index increased 0.3 percent in October after rising 0.1 percent in September. The index for hospital 
services rose 0.8 percent over the month, and the index for physicians' services increased 0.4 percent. The prescription 
drugs index rose 0.3 percent in October. 
The index for used cars and trucks declined 1.2 percent in October after rising 0.7 percent in September. The 
communication index decreased 0.1 percent over the month.
Not seasonally adjusted CPI measures
The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased to an index level of 337.511 (1982-84=100). For the 
month, the index rose 0.2 percent prior to seasonal adjustment. 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) increased to an index level of 331.147 
(1982-84=100). For the month, the index increased 0.1 percent prior to seasonal adjustment. 
For the month, the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U) increased 0.2 percent on a not 
seasonally adjusted basis. Please note that the indexes for the past 10 to 12 months are subject to revision. 
_______________
The Consumer Price Index news release for November 2026 is scheduled to be published on Thursday, December 10, 2026, 
at 8:30 a.m. (ET).
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Upcoming Consumer Price Index Publication Changes
With the publication of January 2027 CPI data on February 11, 2027, several index titles will change: 
"wireless telephone services" will change to "wireless telephone service"; "physicians' services" will change 
to "physician services"; and "music instruments and accessories" will change to "music instruments and 
accessories including instrument rentals." More information is available online at 
www.bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/series-title-changes.htm
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Technical Note
Brief Explanation of the CPI
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services. The CPI reflects
spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S. population. It is based on the expenditures
of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers. Not included in the CPI are the
spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals. Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for
All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U). 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) is based on the expenditures of households
included in the CPI-U definition that meet two requirements: more than one-half of the household's income must come
from clerical or wage occupations, and at least one of the household's earners must have been employed for at least 37
weeks during the previous 12 months. The CPI-W population represents approximately 30 percent of the total U.S.
population and is a subset of the CPI-U population.
The CPIs are based on prices of food, clothing, shelter, fuels, transportation, doctors' and dentists' services, drugs,
and other goods and services that people buy for day-to-day living. Prices are collected each month in 75 urban areas
across the country from about 6,000 housing units and approximately 22,000 retail establishments (department stores,
supermarkets, hospitals, and other types of stores and service establishments). All taxes directly associated with the
purchase and use of items are included in the index. Prices of fuels and a few other items are obtained every month in
all 75 locations. Prices of most other commodities and services are collected every month in the three largest
geographic areas and every other month in other areas. Prices of most goods and services are obtained by personal
visit, telephone call, web, or app collection by the Bureau's trained representatives.
In calculating the index, price changes for the various items in each location are aggregated using weights, which
represent their importance in the spending of the appropriate population group. Local data are then combined to obtain
a U.S. city average. For the CPI-U and CPI-W, separate indexes are also published by size of city, by region of the
country, for cross-classifications of regions and population-size classes, and for 23 selected local areas. Area
indexes do not measure differences in the level of prices among cities; they only measure the average change in prices
for each area since the base period. For the C-CPI-U, data are issued only at the national level. The CPI-U and CPI-W
are considered final when released, but the C-CPI-U is issued in preliminary form and subject to three subsequent
quarterly revisions.

 THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - OCTOBER 2026 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed 
little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in 
professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. 
This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys. The household survey measures labor 
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics. The establishment survey 
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry. For more information about the 
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note. 
Household Survey Data 
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.1 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, 
changed little in October. The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to 
4.3 percent since March. (See table A-1.) 
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates showed little or no change in October for 
adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent), teenagers (13.9 percent), and people who are 
White (3.7 percent), Black (6.6 percent), Asian (2.8 percent), or Hispanic (4.7 percent). (See 
tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.) 
The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more), at 2.0 million, changed 
little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed 
people. (See table A-12.) 
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at 
59.3 percent, changed little in October. These measures have shown little net change since January. 
(See table A-1.) 
The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in 
October. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time 
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs. (See table A-8.) 
In October, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little at 
6.0 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively 
looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job. (See 
table A-1.) 
Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to 
the labor force changed little at 1.6 million in October. These individuals wanted and were 
available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for 
work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the 
marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, also changed little over 
the month at 448,000. (See Summary table A.) 
Establishment Survey Data 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, higher than the average monthly gain 
of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business 
services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. (See table B-1.) 
Employment in professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the 
average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment continued to trend 
up in professional, scientific, and technical services (+33,000), in administrative and support and 
waste management and remediation services (+28,000), and in management of companies and enterprises 
(+9,000). Professional and business services has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 
2025. 
Health care added 42,000 jobs in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the 
prior 12 months. In October, employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home health care 
services (+11,000), and outpatient care centers (+5,000). 
In October, transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and 
messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 
104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) 
contributing most of the gain. 
Manufacturing employment continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 
since a recent low in December 2025. In October, job gains occurred in computer and electronic 
product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000), and primary metal manufacturing 
(+4,000). 
Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, 
quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; wholesale trade; retail trade; information; 
financial activities; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government. 
In October, average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls increased by 14 
cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00. Over the past 12 months, average hourly earnings have increased 
by 3.1 percent. In October, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and nonsupervisory 
employees rose by 12 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $32.75. (See tables B-3 and B-8.) 
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in 
October. In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.5 hours, and overtime edged up 
by 0.1 hour to 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on 
private nonfarm payrolls declined by 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours. (See tables B-2 and B-7.) 
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 
to +186,000, and the change for September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000. With 
these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously 
reported. (Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and government 
agencies since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal factors.)

 PRODUCER PRICE INDEXES - OCTOBER 2026
The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3 percent in October, seasonally adjusted, the 
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Final demand prices advanced 1.4 percent in 
September and 0.4 percent in August. (See table A.) On an unadjusted basis, the index for final 
demand increased 6.5 percent for the 12 months ended in October, the largest 12-month rise 
since moving up 7.4 percent in November 2022.
Leading the October advance in final demand prices, the index for final demand goods increased 
0.5 percent. Prices for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent.
The index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 0.5 percent in October, the 
same as in September. For the 12 months ended in October, prices for final demand less foods, 
energy, and trade services advanced 4.9 percent.
Final Demand
Final demand goods: The index for final demand goods increased 0.5 percent in October following 
a 2.5-percent rise in September. Over 60 percent of the advance in October is attributable to prices 
for final demand goods less foods and energy, which moved up 0.5 percent. The index for final 
demand foods increased 1.3 percent. In contrast, prices for final demand energy edged down 0.1 
percent. For the 12 months ended in October, the index for final demand goods increased 10.2 
percent, the largest 12-month rise since advancing 10.5 percent in October 2022.
Product detail: Within the index for final demand goods in October, prices for basic organic 
chemicals advanced 3.9 percent. The indexes for fresh and dry vegetables; gas fuels; aeronautical, 
nautical, and navigational instruments; jet fuel; and processed young chickens also moved higher. 
(See table 2.) Conversely, diesel fuel prices fell 7.9 percent. The indexes for pork and for passenger 
cars also declined. 
Final demand services: The index for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent in October, the 
fifth consecutive advance. Three-fourths of the October rise can be traced to a 2.0-percent increase in 
prices for final demand transportation and warehousing services. The index for final demand services 
less trade, transportation, and warehousing advanced 0.2 percent. In contrast, margins for final 
demand trade services decreased 0.2 percent.
Product detail: Over 80 percent of the October increase in the index for final demand services is 
attributable to prices for truck transportation of freight, which rose 3.9 percent. The indexes for fuels 
and lubricants retailing; health, beauty, and optical goods retailing; food and alcohol wholesaling; 
hospital outpatient care; and traveler accommodation services also moved higher. Conversely, 
margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling fell 4.2 percent. Prices for system software 
publishing and for airline passenger services also declined.

Intermediate Demand by Commodity Type
Within intermediate demand in October, the index for processed goods increased 0.4 percent, prices 
for unprocessed goods fell 3.1 percent, and the index for services rose 0.6 percent. (See tables B and 
C.)
Processed goods for intermediate demand: Prices for processed goods for intermediate demand 
advanced 0.4 percent in October, the third consecutive rise. Leading the October increase, the index 
for processed materials less foods and energy moved up 0.9 percent. Prices for processed foods and 
feeds advanced 1.0 percent. In contrast, the index for processed energy goods declined 1.6 percent. 
For the 12 months ended in October, prices for processed goods for intermediate demand increased 
14.6 percent, the largest 12-month rise since jumping 17.2 percent in July 2022.
Product detail: More than 40 percent of the October advance in the index for processed goods for 
intermediate demand can be traced to prices for basic organic chemicals, which moved up 3.9 
percent. The indexes for jet fuel, electronic components and accessories, natural gas liquids, 
fabricated structural metal products, and prepared animal feeds also increased. Conversely, prices for 
diesel fuel fell 7.9 percent. The indexes for pork and for lumber also decreased.
Unprocessed goods for intermediate demand: Prices for unprocessed goods for intermediate 
demand fell 3.1 percent in October, the largest decline since moving down 6.6 percent in June. 
Leading the broad-based decrease in October, the index for unprocessed energy materials dropped 
7.7 percent. Prices for unprocessed nonfood materials less energy and for unprocessed foodstuffs and 
feedstuffs also fell, 0.9 percent and 0.2 percent, respectively. For the 12 months ended in October, the 
index for unprocessed goods for intermediate demand rose 16.9 percent.
Product detail: A major factor in the October decline in the index for unprocessed goods for 
intermediate demand was a 10.3-percent decrease in prices for crude petroleum. The indexes for 
corn, slaughter hogs, wheat, aluminum base scrap, and hay and hayseeds also moved down. In 
contrast, prices for raw milk advanced 8.2 percent. The indexes for natural gas and for carbon steel 
scrap also increased.

REAL EARNINGS  OCTOBER 2026 
All employees 
Real average hourly earnings for all employees were unchanged from September to October, seasonally 
adjusted, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. This result stems from an increase of 0.4 
percent in average hourly earnings combined with an increase of 0.4 percent in the Consumer Price 
Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U). 
Real average weekly earnings were unchanged over the month due to no change in real average hourly 
earnings combined with no change in the average workweek. 
******************************************************************************************************** 
* Federal Government Shutdown * 
* * 
* This release usually includes an over-the-year analysis of changes to real earnings. BLS could not * 
* collect the relevant Consumer Price Index data for the October 2025 reference period due to a lapse * 
* in appropriations in late 2025. For that reason, over-the-year comparisons from October 2025 to * 
* October 2026 are not available. * 
* * 
******************************************************************************************************** 
Production and nonsupervisory employees 
Real average hourly earnings for production and nonsupervisory employees increased 0.1 percent from 
September to October, seasonally adjusted. This result stems from a 0.4-percent increase in average 
hourly earnings combined with an increase of 0.3 percent in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage 
Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). 
Real average weekly earnings decreased 0.3 percent over the month due to the change in real average 
hourly earnings combined with a decrease of 0.3 percent in the average workweek. 
___________

U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, September 2026
The U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis announced today that the goods and services deficit was $105.0 billion in September, down $0.7 billion from $105.7 billion in August, revised.

Exports, Imports, and Balance (exhibit 1)
September exports were $321.5 billion, $5.8 billion more than August exports. September imports were $426.6 billion, $5.2 billion more than August imports.
The September decrease in the goods and services deficit reflected a decrease in the goods deficit of $0.7 billion to $135.9 billion and a decrease in the services surplus of less than $0.1 billion to $30.9 billion.
Year-to-date, the goods and services deficit decreased $92.4 billion, or 12.2 percent, from the same period in 2025. Exports increased $297.3 billion or 11.6 percent. Imports increased $204.9 billion or 6.2 percent.
Three-Month Moving Averages (exhibit 2)
The average goods and services deficit increased $11.3 billion to $101.2 billion for the three months ending in September.
Average exports increased $1.4 billion to $316.0 billion in September.
Average imports increased $12.7 billion to $417.2 billion in September.
Year-over-year, the average goods and services deficit increased $36.5 billion from the three months ending in September 2025.
Average exports increased $28.9 billion from September 2025.
Average imports increased $65.4 billion from September 2025.
Exports (exhibits 3, 6, and 7)

Industrial supplies and materials decreased $1.0 billion.
Nonmonetary gold decreased $3.4 billion.

Treatment of Gold in BEA’s International and National Economic Accounts
When incorporating the statistics in this release into BEA’s National Economic Accounts, including Gross Domestic Product, or GDP, BEA replaces exports and imports of nonmonetary gold with an adjustment calculated as the difference between domestic production and industrial use of gold. For additional information, see “How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts?” and “How are exports and imports of nonmonetary gold treated in BEA’s National Economic Accounts?”.
Exports of services increased $0.7 billion to $110.5 billion in September.
Travel increased $0.3 billion.
Charges for the use of intellectual property increased $0.1 billion.
Imports (exhibits 4, 6, and 8)
Imports of goods increased $4.4 billion to $346.9 billion in September.
 Imports of goods on a Census basis increased $8.0 billion.

Real Goods in 2017 Dollars – Census Basis (exhibit 11)
The real goods deficit increased $3.5 billion, or 3.0 percent, to $119.5 billion in September, compared to a 2.2 percent increase in the nominal deficit. (The reason why the Census Basis nominal goods deficit increased, while the BOP nominal goods deficit decreased in September is attributable to a BOP adjustment for nonmonetary gold imports. See “How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts?”.)
Real exports of goods increased $0.2 billion, or 0.1 percent, to $152.2 billion, compared to a 2.5 percent increase in nominal exports.
Real imports of goods increased $3.6 billion, or 1.4 percent, to $271.6 billion, compared to a 2.4 percent increase in nominal imports.
Revisions
Revisions to August exports
Exports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion.
Exports of services were revised up $0.3 billion.
Revisions to August imports
Imports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion.
Imports of services were revised up $0.4 billion.
Goods by Selected Countries and Areas: Monthly – Census Basis (exhibit 19)
The September figures show surpluses, in billions of dollars, with Netherlands ($7.7), South and Central America ($6.2), United Kingdom ($3.0), Hong Kong ($2.5), Australia ($2.1), Brazil ($1.1), Singapore ($0.7), Saudi Arabia ($0.5), and Belgium ($0.2). Deficits were recorded, in billions of dollars, with Mexico ($28.7), Vietnam ($25.3), Taiwan ($21.9), China ($17.9), European Union ($14.2), South Korea ($12.2), Germany ($7.9), Italy ($6.3), Malaysia ($5.3), Japan ($4.8), India ($4.5), Canada ($4.4), Ireland ($3.0), Switzerland ($1.3), France ($1.3), and Israel ($0.7).
The deficit with Taiwan increased $3.6 billion to $21.9 billion in September. Exports increased $0.6 billion to $5.3 billion and imports increased $4.2 billion to $27.3 billion.
The deficit with the European Union increased $3.2 billion to $14.2 billion in September. Exports decreased $0.6 billion to $39.0 billion and imports increased $2.6 billion to $53.2 billion.
The deficit with Canada decreased $2.7 billion to $4.4 billion in September. Exports decreased $0.3 billion to $29.7 billion and imports decreased $3.0 billion to $34.1 billion.
All statistics referenced are seasonally adjusted; statistics are on a balance of payments basis unless otherwise specified. Additional statistics, including not seasonally adjusted statistics and details for goods on a Census basis, are available in exhibits 1-20b of this release. Explanatory Notes
Goods (Census basis)
Data for goods on a Census basis are compiled from the documents collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and reflect the movement of goods between foreign countries and the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and U.S. Foreign Trade Zones. They include government and non-government shipments of goods and exclude shipments between the United States and its territories and possessions; transactions with U.S. military, diplomatic, and consular installations abroad; U.S. goods returned to the United States by its Armed Forces; personal and household effects of travelers; and in-transit shipments. The General Imports value reflects the total arrival of merchandise from foreign countries that immediately enters consumption channels, warehouses, or Foreign Trade Zones.
For imports, the value reported is the CBP-appraised value of merchandise—generally, the price paid for merchandise for export to the United States. Import duties, freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in bringing merchandise to the United States are excluded. The exception is exhibit 17a, which shows CIF import value. The CIF (cost, insurance, and freight) value represents the landed value of the merchandise at the first port of arrival in the United States. It is computed by adding import charges to the customs value and therefore excludes U.S. import duties.
Exports are valued at the f.a.s. (free alongside ship) value of merchandise at the U.S. port of export, based on the transaction price including inland freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in placing the merchandise alongside the carrier at the U.S. port of exportation.

Monthly revisions: Monthly data include actual month's transactions as well as a small number of transactions for previous months. GDP (Advance Estimate), 3rd Quarter 2026
Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the advance estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent.
The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. For more information, refer to the "Technical Notes" below.
Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter.
Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 4.9 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 4.6 percent in the second quarter.
The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 3.0 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 5.6 percent in the second quarter. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, compared with an increase of 5.0 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, compared with an increase of 3.3 percent.

Sources of change for real GDP
Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent (0.8 percent at a quarterly rate 1) in the third quarter, reflecting increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased.
More information on the source data and BEA assumptions that underlie the third-quarter estimate is shown in the key source data and assumptions table.
The increase in investment primarily reflected increases in private inventory investment and in equipment.
The largest contributors to the increase in private inventory investment were wholesale trade and manufacturing (both led by nondurable goods industries), based primarily on Census Bureau inventory book value data.
Within equipment, the increase was led by information processing equipment (mainly computers and peripheral equipment), based primarily on data for imports from the U.S. Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services report and the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September.
The increase in consumer spending reflected increases in both services and goods.
Within services, the increase was led by health care (mainly hospitals and outpatient services), based primarily on U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Current Employment Statistics, and food services and accommodations (mainly purchased meals and beverages), based on Census Bureau Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS) data.
Within goods, the increase was led by other nondurable goods (mainly prescription drugs), based on Census Bureau MRTS data.
Within government spending, the increase was more than accounted for by federal government spending, led by nondefense consumption expenditures. The pattern of nondefense spending primarily reflected sales of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, based on data from the U.S. Department of Energy. Within the National Economic Accounts, sales are deducted from government consumption expenditures. In the third quarter, sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve were less than sales in the second quarter, resulting in an increase in consumption expenditures. Because the oil sold by the government is reflected as an increase in other components of GDP, there is no direct effect on GDP.
Exports and imports primarily reflected Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services data as well as the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September. The decrease in exports primarily reflected a decrease in goods (led by petroleum and related products). The largest contributor to imports was capital goods, except automotive.

How does EIA account for small differences between energy supply and demand data? 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review
Note: Supply = production + imports; demand = consumption + exports; demand - supply = stock change + other 
EIA uses over 60 surveys to collect data on the U.S. energy sector’s supply and demand. In theory, supply and demand should balance. In practice, we often have small differences between our total supply and total demand figures. 
To account for the differences between U.S. total primary energy supply and demand, our Monthly Energy Review includes a stock change and other data series, a grouping of items that account for the differences between supply and demand each month. 
These accounting differences represent a very small share of energy markets. In 2025, our combined surveys accounted for about 128 quadrillion British thermal units (quads) each for U.S. energy supply and demand, and stock change and other was 0.4 quads—about 0.3% of the total. 
Stock change is the net difference between energy held in storage at the beginning and end of a month. 
The other portion of stock change and other represents the many forms of small accounting differences: 
Differences in survey respondent accounting and reporting practices 
Differences in timing between energy activity occurrences and reporting periods 
Measurement and estimation errors 
Limitations in data collection systems and survey coverage 
Energy lost during transfers or storage 
Unreported energy activities 
To document the other differences between supply and demand, besides stock change, we use various adjustments, balancing items, and losses and unaccounted for series, a standard statistical accounting practice. Rather than indicating a flaw in the underlying statistics, these series ensure that published data are consistent and transparent, while also providing a measure of the uncertainty associated with our survey data. 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review
For petroleum and biofuels, our adjustments series accounts for the fact that survey responses may not precisely reflect actual activity. We’ve made improvements to our petroleum data over time to account for changes in transfers to crude oil supply, motor gasoline blending components, distillate fuel oil by pipeline operations, and other developments in petroleum markets. See Appendix B of our Petroleum Supply Monthly for more details. 
For natural gas, our balancing item series accounts for differences between supply and demand. Some of the differences are because of natural gas lost to the atmosphere. Also, there can be differences in conversions of flow data metered at varying temperatures and pressures, variations in company accounting and billing practices, and differences between billing cycles and calendar periods. See Appendix A of our Natural Gas Monthly for more details. 
For coal, we use a losses and unaccounted for series to represent differences in supply and demand, including coal lost during transport and various accounting and timing issues. In 2009, because of incomplete data coverage and different source data, biofuels have a small balancing item to balance biodiesel supply and demand.
